title: Materials world models: Foundation for scientific continuity, emergence, and creation

openalex.abstract_reconstructed_from_inverted_ind: Artificial intelligence for materials science is progressing from isolated prediction and optimization to integrated research systems that connect computation, experimentation, and scientific reasoning. However, the multiscale and path-dependent nature of materials, together with incomplete experimental observations, presents challenges in maintaining scientific continuity across material evolution, evidence, and interpretation. Building on the Materials Genome Initiative, advances in artificial intelligence are transforming materials data, computational tools, and experimental capabilities into the interconnected soft and hard foundations of materials world models (MWMs). The soft foundation integrates physical models, digital twins, materials knowledge, and scientific agents to support prediction and reasoning, while the hard foundation combines automated laboratories, intelligent instruments, and embodied intelligence to enable physical experimentation and validation. Shared material states and persistent evidence memory connect these foundations, allowing new observations to update material representations, evaluate scientific interpretations, and guide subsequent investigations. We examined the scientific foundations, architecture, and emerging capabilities of MWMs, highlighting their potential to support sustained scientific investigation and cumulative knowledge development. Future progress requires AI-native experimental infrastructure, coordinated scientific reasoning, and persistent learning across research campaigns, together with evaluation frameworks that assess scientific continuity and knowledge transfer. Through sustained interaction with physical materials and experimental evidence, MWMs may progressively revise existing scientific understanding, reveal previously unrecognized mechanisms, and enable the creation of new hypotheses, material concepts, and processing strategies. Their development offers a pathway toward physically grounded, evidence-driven, and increasingly autonomous materials research.
